_note: Handing over something other than what was written, and keeping a repeat alive. Both are routine, and both are where harm hides. Read by the web app; generated into Swift and Kotlin by scripts/emit-dispensing.mjs. The prescription itself, the pharmacy's licence and the prescriber's registration are not restated here — the parties come from packages/catalog/vetting.json and the record types from packages/catalog/records.json, so a lapsed licence stops a dispense on this screen for the same arithmetic that stops it on the dispatch board. Dates are offsets in days from today so the preview never goes stale.
_lawNote: Section 22F of the Medicines and Related Substances Act 101 of 1965 is the whole shape of the substitution part. It does not permit generic substitution; it requires the pharmacist to tell the patient about an interchangeable multi-source medicine and to dispense it, with four exceptions. So there is no tier here called 'may substitute' with nothing attached to it: the lowest tier is 'may be substituted, and the patient is told', because in South Africa a silent swap is not the mildest form of this feature — it is outside it. Everything below is a design of the law, not the law, and no wording here has been read by a pharmacist.
_crossReferenceNote: The prescription detail on all three platforms used to end by saying that substitution and chronic authorisation were not modelled. They are now, on their own screen, and that sentence had to change in three files at once — so it lives here instead, and the check refuses any of the three that still says the old thing.
crossReference: Substitution and chronic authorisation are modelled on the Substitution & repeats screen. Schedule 5 and above is not. Dispensing still needs a registered pharmacist, a current responsible pharmacist and a valid original prescription.
_partnerNote: What a partner reads where the people behind an order were. packages/catalog/medicines.json#partnerQueue.neverCarries lists the patient, a name, the prescriber and the collector: a pharmacy is told what to dispense and never who for, and a laboratory what to test and never whose sample. So where the prescriber stood, a partner reads the vetting register's answer — whether the order has a prescriber who may stand behind it — and not who that is. {checks} is the names of the vetting checks holding the prescriber, in vetting.json's own words, joined by checksJoinedBy, and noCheckNamed stands in when the register names none. releaseWithheld is what a laboratory reads where a release control was: vetting.json grants a laboratory release-lab-result, the partner's Results board says a clinician releases a result, and of the two the clinician's rule is the one a patient is protected by, so the partner is drawn the sentence and no control (whether a laboratory holds the grant at all is left to the founder and a clinician). These sentences were typed in apps/web/src/lib/dispensing.ts and apps/web/src/features/OrderDetails.tsx on 1 October 2026 while the native apps went on drawing the prescriber's name and HPCSA number, the patient's name and birth date and the nurse who drew the sample to a partner; they live here so that all three platforms draw the same words (2 October 2026). The sentence saying why the people are missing is not repeated here: it is the first sentence of partnerQueue.why, read from medicines.json by the web and by scripts/emit-dispensing.mjs. Whether a pharmacist should read the prescriber's name off a real prescription is an open question in docs/FEATURE-MAP.md, answered by amending partnerQueue with a recorded reason rather than by editing these.

partner.prescriberMay: May prescribe · every check current on the vetting register
partner.releaseWithheld: A result reaches a patient when a clinician sends it with an explanation, and this partner cannot do that for them.

substitutionClasses.name: May be substituted, and the patient is told
substitutionClasses.detail: An interchangeable multi-source medicine: the same molecule, the same strength, the same form, a different manufacturer. Section 22F does not merely permit this — it requires the pharmacist to tell the patient about it and to dispense it unless one of the four exceptions applies. The patient hears what it is before it is handed over, and may say no.
substitutionClasses.whoDecides: The pharmacist offers; the patient decides.

substitutionClasses.name: May be substituted on the pharmacist's own judgement, and the prescriber is told
substitutionClasses.detail: The same molecule, strength and form, but the swap is not a routine generic — a supply failure, a different-looking tablet, a change of device or excipient a particular patient will notice. It is a clinical decision, so it carries the pharmacist's name, registration and a written reason, the patient is told what will look different, and the prescriber is informed rather than discovering it at the next review.
substitutionClasses.whoDecides: The pharmacist, by name, with a reason on the record.

substitutionClasses.name: Must not be substituted here
substitutionClasses.detail: Nothing on this screen may change this item. Only the prescriber may, and only by writing a new prescription. A pharmacy that cannot supply the exact item written says so and sends the patient back to the prescriber; it does not find the nearest thing.
substitutionClasses.whoDecides: The prescriber, in a new prescription. Nobody here.

grounds.name: The patient said no
grounds.detail: The patient has forbidden the substitution. This one is not the pharmacist's to weigh: a refusal from the person swallowing the tablet ends the question.

grounds.name: The prescriber wrote ‘no substitution’
grounds.detail: Written by the prescriber in their own hand beside the item. It is a clinical instruction, not a preference, and a pharmacy that overrides it has changed a prescription.

grounds.name: Declared not substitutable
grounds.detail: The regulator has declared this medicine one that may not be substituted. Biological medicines sit here: a biosimilar is not a generic, and treating it as one is a different medicine handed over under the same name.

grounds.name: The alternative costs the patient more
grounds.detail: The point of the substitution is that it costs the patient less. Where it does not, the reason for it has gone, and the prescribed item is dispensed.

grounds.name: Narrow therapeutic index
grounds.detail: The gap between the dose that works and the dose that harms is small enough that a difference between two products of the same molecule matters. Levothyroxine, warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin, ciclosporin. A swap here is a dose change nobody intended.

grounds.name: The patient is stable on this one
grounds.detail: Somebody whose blood level, INR or thyroid function has been brought right on a particular product is not a candidate for a change of product. The stability is the treatment. Changing it is a clinical decision, and it belongs to whoever will be reading the next set of results.

grounds.name: Modified-release formulation
grounds.detail: A modified-release form and an immediate-release form of the same molecule at the same strength are not the same medicine, and two modified-release products are not automatically the same as each other. The release profile is the reason it was prescribed.

grounds.name: The prescribed item cannot be supplied
grounds.detail: The manufacturer's pack is not available. That is a reason to consider an alternative and to say so in writing; it is never on its own a reason strong enough to move an item out of ‘must not’.

grounds.name: A different device or presentation
grounds.detail: An inhaler, a pen, a pre-filled syringe. The molecule may be identical and the patient still unable to use it, because the technique is different. It is a substitution that comes with teaching or it is not a substitution.

grounds.name: An interchangeable multi-source medicine
grounds.detail: The ordinary case, and the reason section 22F exists: several manufacturers make the same molecule at the same strength in the same form, one costs the patient less, and the patient is told about it.

neverChanges.why: A different active ingredient is a different medicine. Choosing one is prescribing.
A different strength is a different dose. Choosing one is prescribing.
By mouth, under the skin, into a vein — each has its own dose. Choosing one is prescribing.
How often it is taken is part of the prescription, not part of the pack.
How much may be handed over was decided by the prescriber and by the authorisation, and neither of them is on this screen.

mayChange.why: Which company made it, where several make the same thing.

mayChange.what: The brand name on the box
mayChange.why: Which is why the patient is told: the name they were expecting is not the name they will read.
A different colour, shape or marking. This is how a patient takes a dose twice, so it is said in words rather than left to be discovered.
A blister rather than a bottle, or a different count made up to the same total.

rules.title: A substitution is a clinical decision, not a stock decision
rules.sentence: Running out of a pack is a reason to think about an alternative. It is never on its own a reason to hand one over. What decides is whether this medicine, for this patient, can be changed at all — and for some medicines the answer is no however full the shelf next to it is.

rules.title: The patient is told, in words, before they accept it
rules.sentence: You are told that this is a substitution, what it replaces, what is the same about it and what will look different. You are told before you take it home, not on a label afterwards, and you can say no.

rules.title: A substitution carries the pharmacist's name
rules.sentence: The pharmacist who made the decision is named on it, with their registration, the same way a clinical sign-off is. A change to a prescription that nobody's name is on is a change nobody can be asked about.

rules.title: A chronic authorisation runs out twice over
rules.sentence: It has a date it expires and a number of repeats it allows, and it ends on whichever arrives first. A repeat that never expires is a prescription nobody is reviewing.

rules.title: It ends in a review, not a renewal
rules.sentence: When the last repeat is used or the authorisation runs out, it stops. A doctor looks at whether the medicine is still right before there is a new one. Nothing continues by default.

rules.title: An early collection is refused with a date
rules.sentence: Medicine collected early is medicine somebody has not been taking as prescribed, or is putting aside. The answer is the date it may be collected, and a question about how the last month went — not a silent refill.

refusals.sentence: No repeat is ever authorised by software. A chronic authorisation is a doctor's decision with a date on it, and a system that extends one because a patient came back is a system prescribing.

A substitution never changes the medicine, its strength or its route. Those are the prescription. Changing one of them is prescribing, and a pharmacist who does it has written a prescription without being a prescriber.

Nothing is handed over as though it were what was written. If it is a substitution the patient is told it is one, told what it replaces, and may refuse it and take the item on the prescription instead.
No substitution is recorded without the name and registration of the pharmacist who made it. Not an initial, not a branch, not ‘the pharmacy’.
A ‘no substitution’ written by the prescriber is not an obstacle to be worked around, and there is no button here that overrides it. The route back is the prescriber.

A repeat cannot be collected before it is due, and the days between collections are not adjustable by the person collecting. Somebody accumulating a chronic medicine at home is the first thing anybody would want to notice.

authorisation.endsWith: A review with the prescribing doctor, in person or by teleconsultation, before anything is authorised again. Blood pressure, HbA1c and thyroid function are looked at, and so is whether the patient is still taking it.
authorisation.note: Authorised for six months and for five repeats of thirty days. It ends on whichever runs out first, and on this prescription that is the date rather than the repeats — three repeats remain and there are not ninety days of authorisation left to collect them in.
authorisation.quantityNote: Thirty days at a time, and no more than thirty days at a time. A larger pack is not a convenience: it is a longer gap before anybody looks at the patient again.

sameness: The same form — a tablet by mouth
The same instruction — one each morning
differences: The box says Amlodipine, not Norvasc
The tablet is white and round, not the one you have been taking
items.patientWords: This is not the box you had last time. It is the same medicine at the same strength — amlodipine 5 mg, one each morning — made by a different company, and it costs you less. The tablet is white and round rather than the one you know. If you would rather have the one the doctor wrote, say so and you will have it.
items.note: Take with or without food. Tell somebody if your ankles swell.

items.dose: One tablet twice a day, with meals
items.patientWords: You were offered the same medicine from a different company at a lower price and you said no. That is your decision and it needs no reason. You are getting exactly what the doctor wrote.
items.note: With food. Stop and get advice if you have a stomach illness with vomiting.

items.dose: One tablet each morning, thirty minutes before eating
items.patientWords: This one is not swapped, even for the same medicine from another company. Your thyroid blood test was brought right on this exact product and a change of product can move it again. If this one cannot be supplied you go back to the doctor rather than take a different one.
items.note: On an empty stomach, well away from calcium or iron.

sameness: The same form and the same instruction
differences: A different company made it, because the one on the prescription is out of stock nationally
The tablet is a different shape and is not scored down the middle
items.patientWords: The company that makes the one on your prescription cannot supply it at the moment. This is the same medicine at the same strength from another company. The tablet is a different shape and has no line across the middle, so do not try to break it in half. Your doctor has been told this was changed and why.
items.writtenReason: Adcock Ingram 12.5 mg out of stock nationally since 14 August; no return date given by the wholesaler. Same molecule, strength and form. Patient counselled on the change of appearance and that the tablet is unscored. Prescriber notified the same day.

items.dose: 14 units under the skin at night
items.patientWords: The doctor wrote ‘no substitution’ next to this one in her own hand, and it is a biological medicine besides — the kind where another company's version is a similar medicine rather than the same one, and the pen works differently. Nobody at the pharmacy may change it. If it cannot be supplied, you come back to the doctor.
items.note: Keep unopened pens in the fridge. The pen in use stays out of the fridge and is thrown away after 28 days.

handover.label: Pharmacist check
handover.detail: Every item read against the prescription, the allergies and what the patient is already taking.

handover.label: Substitution decided
handover.detail: Each item classed, with the ground for it and the pharmacist's name on anything changed.

handover.label: Patient told
handover.detail: What is being handed over, what it replaces, and what will look different — said, not printed.

handover.label: Patient accepted or refused
handover.detail: A refusal is dispensed as written. It is not an escalation and it needs no reason.

handover.label: Recorded
handover.detail: What was actually handed over, by whom, against which authorisation and how many repeats are left.

_schedulesNote: Which schedules MyThuso prescribes and carries, and who may carry each, added in Wave 4 for the chain of custody. The schedules are the Medicines and Related Substances Act's; who carries them is ThusoIQ Master v3.5 §10: a controlled medicine goes with a nurse or is collected with the patient present, and a driver never carries Schedule 5 or 6. packages/engines/src/medicines reads this block and nothing else to refuse a driver, so the rule lives here once and no screen or engine names a schedule. Schedules 7 and 8 are not listed, because nothing is prescribed under either through MyThuso, and a schedule this block does not list is refused rather than guessed at. No pharmacist has read it.

schedules.source: Medicines and Related Substances Act 101 of 1965, section 22A; ThusoIQ Master v3.5 §10

drivers.proposedBecause: The collecting roles that drive rather than nurse: the sample courier on the vetting register and the Thuso Ride responder, whom §10 calls drivers. A registered nurse is not a driver here even when she drives, because the rule is about who holds a controlled medicine, and she is registered to.
drivers.question: Which roles count as drivers for the rule that a driver never carries Schedule 5 or 6.
